unit.title: Crypto risks and reality
unit.description: Volatility, collapses, scams, yields and how much crypto weighs in a portfolio

texts: Four years in bitcoin
Late 2016: you go in with **€1,000** in bitcoin. Live it week by week with **real data**; you can sell whenever you like.
In December 2017, bitcoin hits a high after multiplying 19 times in a year. How far did it fall from there?
20 %, like a bad patch on the stock market
Around 40 %
More than four fifths
On weekly closes, from $19,141 in December 2017 to $3,253 a year later: **−83 %**. It didn't get back to that high until November 2020.
Make it to the end, whether you sell or not.
Anyone who held on multiplied their money 33 times in four years, after going through a **−83 %** fall from the high. In crypto, that rollercoaster is the norm, not the exception.
You've sold. See what happens next…
From €1,000 to about €33,000, with a −83 % along the way.
Your €1,000 is worth less than €850. Can you hold on?
It's shooting up like a rocket! What if it falls just as fast?
Hit «Start». You can sell whenever you like
«It only has to rise 75 %»
Dani
I bought at the top and I'm down 75 %.
No stress: as soon as it rises 75 %, I'll have my money back.
How much does it have to rise to get back to where it started?
75 %, the same as it fell
If €100 drops to €25, a +75 % leaves you at €43.75.
You have to multiply by 4: **+300 %**.
300 %: you have to multiply by 4
Exactly! To get from 25 to 100 you multiply by 4: **+300 %**.
150 %, double
Not enough: to get from 25 to 100 you multiply by 4, a **+300 %**.
And after a −90 %, you need **+900 %**.
Many cryptos fell more than 90 % and never came back.

steps.title: Volatility in numbers
steps.body:
Bitcoin had already fallen more than **80 %** in 2014-2015 and in 2018; winning back its late-2017 high took about **3 years**.

Its annual volatility is around **50-80 %**, compared with 15 % for a global stock index: a −10 % week is common. It's a highly volatile asset, no guarantee scheme covers it and **you can lose everything you invest**.
steps.key: In crypto, falls of 70 % and years of waiting to recover are part of the history.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, open Bitcoin and compare its chart with the S&P 500's.

texts: A week in November 2022
Álex
Álex keeps their crypto on FTX, one of the biggest exchanges in the world.
And they pay me interest for leaving it there. What could go wrong?
News breaks that Alameda, FTX's sister company, relies heavily on the FTT token.
Everyone's pulling their money out and withdrawals are slow…
What would you do in Álex's shoes?
Wait: it's too big to fail
Big isn't the same as solvent. And the worst happened.
Try to withdraw now: slow withdrawals are a warning sign
Well spotted. If someone else holds your crypto, you take on their risk too.
Deposit more to earn more interest
If the platform's in trouble, that interest is worth nothing.
8 November: FTX freezes withdrawals. On the 11th, it files for bankruptcy.
FTX had passed its customers' money to Alameda.
Álex is now just another creditor, in a process that takes years.
Who holds your crypto?
When you leave your crypto on a platform, you depend on it being **solvent and honest**. Does this reduce that risk or increase it?
Reduces it
Increases it
Platform authorised under MiCA
MiCA requires platforms to be authorised and to keep customers' assets separate.
Everything on a single platform
If that platform goes down, you lose it all in one go.
Keeps your crypto separate from its own money
If it goes bust, what's yours doesn't get mixed up with its debts. FTX mixed them.
Pays you 8 % for leaving your crypto there
A high yield just for depositing usually means it's lending out or risking your money.
Knowing who holds your crypto
If someone else holds it, you take on their risk: get to know them.
Ignoring that withdrawals take days
Slow withdrawals were FTX's warning sign.
Sort the six situations.
If someone else holds your crypto, you take on **counterparty risk**: you depend on them being solvent and honest. And in crypto there's no guarantee scheme like the one for bank deposits.
Hint: does it leave you more exposed if the platform goes down?
Going well! Think about what happened to Álex.
Reduces the risk or increases it? Sort each case

steps.title: What changed
steps.body:
Sam Bankman-Fried, founder of FTX, was sentenced in 2024 to **25 years** in prison for fraud.

MiCA now requires platforms to be authorised and to keep customers' assets separate. Even so, in crypto there's no guarantee scheme like the one for bank deposits: it pays to know who holds your crypto and not to keep it all on one platform. And remember: **you can lose everything you invest**.
steps.key: If someone else holds your crypto, you also take on their risk of bankruptcy or fraud.
steps.tip: Ask your tutor Lumi what happens to your shares if your broker goes bust.

texts: A trendy token
Nico
There's a new token inspired by a TV series. It's taking off!
The creators are anonymous, but people in the group say it'll do x100.
What do you tell Nico?
Get in fast, before it goes up even more
Urgency and promises of x100: two classic signs of a trap.
Not without knowing who's behind it or whether you'll be able to sell
Nice! Anonymous creators and x100 promises are red flags.
Put in just a little, just in case
If it's a trap, that little bit is lost completely.
It really happened in 2021 with the SQUID token: it shot up and, within minutes, crashed to almost zero.
On top of that, buyers couldn't sell: a textbook **rug pull**.
Creating a token takes minutes: thousands appear every day, and nearly all end up worthless.
Three traps, one ending
Almost every token scam follows one of these three scripts. Which is which?
Rug pull
Pump and dump
Fake airdrop
The creators pull the liquidity and disappear
They «pull the rug»: suddenly investors have nothing to stand on.
A group pumps up the price with ads and sells to latecomers
First they pump the price, then they dump on the last ones in.
«Free tokens»: connect your wallet and sign to claim them
That signature can give permission to empty your wallet.
Paid influencers: «buy NOW, it's going to do x100»
The hype pumps up the price so the organisers can sell high.
The token shoots up and, within minutes, its creators sell everything
Like SQUID: the creators take the money and abandon the project.
Tokens you never bought show up, with a website to swap them
They're bait: the website asks you to sign a malicious permission.
Sort the six traps.
Three traps with the same ending: **your money ends up in someone else's pocket**. If the only reason to buy is that «it's going to go up», maybe someone wants to sell to you.
Hint: do they disappear, pump the price or ask you to sign?
Going well! Notice who ends up with the money.
Sort each trap

steps.title: The red flags
steps.body:
A **memecoin** starts life as a joke or a fad (Dogecoin, in 2013, as a joke): many have no use at all and their price depends only on attention.

Red flags: anonymous creators with no track record, promises of «x100», urgency, paid influencers, not being able to sell, being asked to connect your wallet or share your seed phrase. With these tokens **you can lose everything you invest** in minutes.
steps.key: If the only reason to buy is that «it's going to go up», someone probably wants to sell to you.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, search for Dogecoin and see how far it has fallen from its peak.

u13l4.title: Staking and DeFi: where the yield comes from

texts: Interest for lending your crypto
Sara
A platform pays me very high interest for leaving my crypto with it. It says it lends it out and gives me a share.
They call it a «savings account». It sounds like a bank, so there's no risk, right?
What do you ask Sara first?
What's the most I can deposit?
Before «how much», ask **where from**. If nobody explains it, be suspicious.
Who does it lend my crypto to, and what happens if they don't give it back?
That's the question. If whoever receives it doesn't pay, the platform can't pay you either.
Do I earn more if I bring my friends?
Earning for bringing people in is the classic sign of a pyramid scheme.
June 2022: Celsius, one of the biggest platforms of this kind, freezes withdrawals. A month later it files for bankruptcy.
It wasn't a bank: there was no guarantee fund covering its customers.
If you don't know where the yield comes from, maybe the yield is you.
Staking: does it protect you from the price?

With **staking** you lock up your coins to validate blocks (on Ethereum, for example) and the network pays you **in the same crypto**; if the validator fails, you can lose part of it (*slashing*). You have **€1,000** in ether.
ether
You earn 3 % from staking, paid in ether, and ether falls 40 % against the euro. Where do you end up?
Ahead: staking protects me
Down almost 40 %
Where I started
1.03 × 0.60 = 0.618: your €1,000 shrinks to **€618**. The 3 % is paid in a coin that's worth less.
With ether down 40 %, find the yield you'd need to break even.
To make up for a 40 % fall you'd need a **67 %** yield. **Staking doesn't protect you from the price**: it just gives you more units of the same thing.
Yields like that in crypto usually hide a lot of risk… or a trap.
In the red: that's what *slashing* looks like, if the validator fails.
You've got more coins, but each one is worth less.
Lower the price of ether and see what you're left with in euros
Who pays the interest?
Every yield comes from somewhere: place each one by **who pays it**. In DeFi there are also code bugs and hacks.
The network
The borrower
Those who join later
Reward for validating blocks on Ethereum
It's staking: the network pays with new coins and fees.
Interest on a collateralised DeFi loan
The borrower pays it, through a smart contract.
«30 % a month, risk-free» that nobody can explain
If nobody can explain where it comes from, it may come from newcomers' money.
Fees from transactions on the network
They're part of the validator's reward.
You earn more for every friend you bring
It's the classic sign of a pyramid scheme.
A platform that lends your crypto to others
It pays you part of what it charges borrowers… and risks your money.
Place the six yields.

**Who pays the interest, and why?** If nobody can explain it, it may come from those who join later, and in crypto **you can lose everything**. Try it: ask your tutor Lumi where a yield you've seen comes from.
Ask yourself: whose pocket is that money coming out of?
Nice! Explainable doesn't mean risk-free, but the unexplainable usually ends badly.
Who pays? Place each yield
Iker's ETP
Iker
At last I can buy bitcoin like a share, with my broker! It's up 50 % this month.
Two months later, bitcoin falls 30 %. So does Iker's ETP.
Wasn't this a regulated product? I'm selling it all before it falls further.
What's happened to Iker?
He's been unlucky with the product
The ETP did the same as bitcoin. The problem was when he bought and when he sold.
He bought in euphoria and sold in panic
Exactly. It has a name: the **behaviour gap**.
He should have bought bitcoin directly
The wrapper wouldn't have changed the fall or how he reacted.
According to Morningstar, that's how investors lost about 14 points a year compared with the ETF itself.
With assets this volatile, the biggest risk is usually our own behaviour.
Directly or on the stock market
You can hold bitcoin **directly** (on an exchange or keeping it yourself) or through an **ETP** that tracks its price and trades on the stock market. Which does each feature belong to?
Directly
ETP on the stock market
Both
Trades 24 hours, 7 days a week
The crypto market never closes; the stock market has opening hours.
You buy it with your usual broker
It's an exchange-traded product: you buy it like a share.
If you keep the keys yourself and lose the seed phrase, it's gone
With self-custody, nobody can recover them for you.
Issuer and custodian risk
An ETP is a security from an issuer, backed by crypto held by a custodian.
Charges an annual fee
Like any exchange-traded product, it has management costs.
If bitcoin falls 70 %, it falls just as much
The wrapper doesn't change what's inside.
Sort the six features.
The wrapper changes the custody, the trading hours and the paperwork, **not the volatility**: if bitcoin falls 70 %, so does the ETP.
Hint: who holds the keys in each case?
Nice! You swap one risk for another, but the price is the same.
Directly, ETP or both? Sort each feature

steps.title: In Europe: ETPs and ETNs
steps.body:
In the US, **spot bitcoin ETFs** were approved in January 2024, but many can't be bought from the EU because they don't have a KID.

UCITS rules don't allow a fund holding a single crypto, so in Europe they're sold as **ETPs** or **ETNs**: debt securities from an issuer, usually **backed** by the crypto held by a custodian. On top, you take on issuer and custodian risk, plus an annual fee. **You can lose everything you invest**.
steps.key: A crypto ETP saves you from looking after keys, but it doesn't save you a single point of volatility.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, search for the IBIT ETF and compare its chart with Bitcoin's.

u13l6.title: How much crypto in a portfolio

texts: A 5 % that doesn't stay at 5 %
January 2015: you split **€10,000** between US shares and bonds (real data). Add a little bitcoin and see what happens up to 2025 **without touching anything**.
US shares (S&P 500)
US bonds
Bitcoin
With just 5 % in bitcoin and without touching anything until 2025, what was the whole portfolio's worst fall?
Same as without bitcoin: −22 %
A bit worse: −30 %
Much worse: more than −60 %
Bitcoin grew so much that the 5 % ended up being almost the whole portfolio. When it fell in 2022, it dragged the total down: **−66 %**.
Put 5 % in bitcoin and look at the worst fall.
Without rebalancing, **crypto's weight grows by itself**, and so does the risk: that 5 % grew to almost 90 % of the portfolio. The worst fall went from −22 % to −66 %.
With this much bitcoin, your portfolio now moves like bitcoin.
A 5 % that ends up running the whole portfolio. Did you see that coming?
Raise bitcoin to 5 % and look at the worst fall
Rebalancing: back to your 5 %
The same portfolio, but now **every year** you sell whatever has grown too big and go back to your weights. How much bitcoin can you hold without the worst fall going past −25 %?
US shares (S&P 500)
US bonds
Bitcoin
Hold some bitcoin without the worst fall going past −25 %.
By rebalancing, your 5 % goes back to being 5 % every year: the worst fall stays at **−23 %**. And remember: bitcoin is the one that survived; many other cryptos ended up at zero.
Too much: at that weight, the fall really hurts.
That's it! Some bitcoin, with the risk kept on a leash.
Raise bitcoin bit by bit and keep an eye on the worst fall

steps.title: The part you could lose
steps.body:
With 5 % in crypto, a 75 % fall knocks **3.75 %** off the total; with 50 %, **37.5 %**.

People who decide to hold crypto usually write into their plan: first, the **cushion** and no expensive debt; a **maximum** they could lose entirely without it changing their life; and when to **rebalance**. These are examples of how people think it through, not personalised recommendations. In crypto **you can lose everything you invest**.
steps.key: Crypto's weight in the total, not its potential, decides how much it can hurt you.
steps.tip: Try it: open your Portfolio and see what percentage you have in crypto today.

u13l1-2.prompt: One of the big cryptocurrencies, in daily candlesticks. What did it do over the next 10 sessions?
u13l1-2.explanation: In crypto, moves of 10-15 % in two weeks are common, in either direction.

u13l1-3.prompt: Another big cryptocurrency, in daily candlesticks. Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u13l1-3.explanation: Guessing the next move of such a volatile asset is a lot like tossing a coin.

u13l1-8.prompt: Laura bought bitcoin at a peak and is down 60 %. She reads on social media that "it always recovers". What does she think?
options: That she doesn't know if or when it will recover
That she should buy more now to lower her average price
That it will definitely recover, as always
u13l1-8.explanation: When prices drop sharply, what helps is a plan made calmly, not slogans from social media.
feedback: Good: nobody knows whether it will get back to its peak; that's why position size is decided beforehand.
Averaging down on an asset that can keep falling increases what you have at risk: it doesn't fix the loss.
Bitcoin has recovered in the past after years; many other cryptos never have. The past guarantees nothing.

u13l1-10.prompt: Order from lowest to highest typical volatility.
u13l1-10.explanation: Less than 1 %, 4-7 %, around 15 % and 50-80 % a year.

u13l1-12.prompt: You have €10,000 and don't want to risk more than 1% (€100) on bitcoin. Place the stop below the last low and choose the amount.
u13l1-12.explanation: In such a volatile asset the stop sits far from the price, so the amount comes out small. That way, even if the stop is hit, you only lose €100. The temptation is to buy a lot and put the stop very close, but any normal swing will trigger it.

u13l2-1.prompt: Put in order what happened with FTX in November 2022.
options: It's reported that Alameda, its sister company, relies heavily on the FTT token
u13l2-1.explanation: It all happened in about ten days: trust took years to build and days to break.

options: That the price of what you hold falls
That whoever holds your money doesn't give it back
That you send your crypto to the wrong address by mistake
u13l2-2.explanation: It doesn't depend on the asset, but on the company you're trusting.

u13l2-3.prompt: If you leave your crypto on an exchange that goes bust, a guarantee scheme pays you back up to €100,000.
u13l2-3.explanation: That scheme exists for bank deposits; there's nothing equivalent for crypto.

u13l2-6.prompt: Ana has €1,000 in crypto on an exchange authorised under MiCA and €9,000 in an index fund. A friend tells her that, after FTX, "all exchanges are scams". What does she reply?
options: That the risk exists, but it can be reduced
That with MiCA the risk is zero
That he's right: no exchange can be trusted, authorised or not
u13l2-6.explanation: Between "it's all a scam" and "there's no risk" lies the useful part: measuring and limiting the risk.
feedback: Good: it doesn't remove the risk, but it limits it. And she knows she could lose that €1,000.
MiCA reduces risks, it doesn't remove them, and it doesn't protect you from price moves.
One platform committing fraud doesn't mean they all do; what's useful is knowing what risk you're taking.

u13l2-7.prompt: Match each case with what it teaches.
u13l2-7.explanation: Three real blows and Europe's regulatory response.
right: An exchange can lose its customers' crypto
Requires authorisation and keeping assets separate
An exchange can misuse its customers' money

u13l2-9.prompt: If someone else holds your money, you take on ____ risk.
u13l2-9.explanation: It's the risk that the other party doesn't hold up its end.

u13l3-1.prompt: Select the messages that are scams or a clear sign of a rug pull.
options: Congratulations, you've got $2,000 in free tokens. Connect your wallet and sign to claim them.
I've read the CNMV guide on crypto-assets, shall we talk about it?

Not financial advice 😉 but I've gone all in on this coin I launched yesterday.
u13l3-1.explanation: Urgency, promises of x100, gifts that ask you to sign and a creator promoting their own coin are classic signs.

u13l3-2.prompt: Which are red flags in a new token? Select all that apply.
options: Being listed on several authorised exchanges
Its code being published and audited
Not letting you sell after you buy
Anonymous creators with no track record
u13l3-2.explanation: Not being able to sell and anonymous creators are red flags, as are promises of going x100. Audited code or a listing on authorised platforms guarantees nothing, but it isn't a red flag.

u13l3-4.prompt: Pablo sees a new token that has gone up 2,000 % in two days. In a group chat everyone says there's still plenty of upside. What does he do?
options: Puts in just a little, so he doesn't miss out
Stays out: he doesn't know what it is or who's behind it
Puts his savings in: everyone says there's still plenty of time
u13l3-4.explanation: Buying just because something has gone up a lot is what drives pump and dumps.
feedback: Even a little means buying something he doesn't understand out of fear of missing out: the likeliest outcome is losing it.
Good: if the only argument is that it's going up, the risk of losing everything is huge.
He arrives just as the early buyers want to sell: the classic pump-and-dump victim.

u13l3-9.explanation: It's the best-known memecoin: its price depends mainly on the attention it gets.

u13l3-10.prompt: Inflating the price with hype to sell to latecomers is called pump and ____.
u13l3-10.explanation: Pump (inflate) and dump (offload): latecomers buy what the organisers are selling.

u13l4-4.prompt: Where does the staking yield come from?
u13l4-4.explanation: It's the reward the network pays for validating blocks.

u13l4-5.prompt: In a DeFi loan, the interest you earn is paid by the borrower.
u13l4-5.explanation: That's why the risk also depends on the borrower's collateral and the contract's code.

u13l4-7.prompt: Match each source of yield with who pays it.
u13l4-7.explanation: If you can't fill in this column for a product, you don't know where what you're paid comes from.
right: The bank, which lends that money to others
The network, with new coins and fees

u13l4-8.prompt: What risks come with putting your crypto into DeFi? Select all that apply.
options: Your bank raising its custody fee
The Guarantee Fund taking a while to pay you back
u13l4-8.explanation: In DeFi there's no bank and no guarantee fund: if the platform is hacked or the contract has a bug, there's no cushion. And the crypto's price can fall as well.

options: You earn more for every friend you bring in

u13l4-10.explanation: Explainable doesn't mean risk-free, but the unexplainable almost always ends badly.

u13l5-5.prompt: Pablo wants exposure to bitcoin, but he's afraid of losing his keys. Which option does he consider, and what risk is he left with?
options: An ETP, which removes all risks
A "guaranteed bitcoin fund" someone offers him over the phone

Be wary of any "guarantee" on crypto, especially from someone who calls you out of the blue.

u13l5-9.prompt: In Europe, listed products tracking a single crypto are usually ETPs or ____.

options: Sending it to the wrong address
u13l5-10.explanation: With an ETP you don't manage keys or addresses: the custodian does. You're left with bitcoin's volatility and issuer and custodian risk, plus an annual fee.

u13l6-1.prompt: Split up a sample €10,000 portfolio over 20 years. The written plan says: crypto at most 5 % in total, at least 20 % in bonds and no asset above 60 %.
u13l6-1.explanation: Everyone sets the rules in their own plan; here they're for practice. Note that the crypto limit is bitcoin and ethereum added together.

u13l6-6.prompt: Pablo is 22, has no emergency fund and owes €2,000 on his credit card. He wants to put €3,000 into crypto "because he's young and can take risks". What does he bear in mind?
options: That he should put in just half and cut the debt with the rest
That the emergency fund and expensive debt come first
That being young, the more risk he takes, the better
u13l6-6.explanation: Age gives you time, but it doesn't replace the basics: an emergency fund and no expensive debt.
feedback: Better than putting it all in, but he'd still have expensive debt and no emergency fund: any surprise would force him to sell.
Good: the order matters. Credit card debt costs high interest for sure; crypto can be lost entirely.
With no cushion and expensive debt, a sharp fall could force him to sell at the worst moment or borrow even more.

u13l6-7.prompt: Put in order the steps before holding crypto in a portfolio.
options: A written plan with a maximum for crypto
Rebalancing if it goes over the maximum
u13l6-7.explanation: First the basics; then written rules; and finally, sticking to them when the market moves.

u13l6-10.prompt: Lumi has read that someone got rich by putting everything into crypto and asks why not do the same. What do you tell her?
options: Because you only see the ones who won
Go for it: if it worked for him, it'll work for you
u13l6-10.explanation: The success stories going around are a biased sample: losses don't get posted.
feedback: Not that either: it can rise a lot. The problem is not being able to afford for it to drop to zero.
That's it! It's survivorship bias: people who lost everything don't usually share it on social media.
One person getting lucky says nothing about the odds.
lines: I read that someone put everything into crypto and got rich 🤑

u13l6-11.prompt: You have 5% of your portfolio in crypto. If that crypto goes to zero, what is the most your portfolio can lose?
u13l6-11.explanation: The most you can lose on one part is what that part weighs in the total. That's why the weight is decided before buying. The temptation is to think that a crypto going to zero drags down the whole portfolio, and it doesn't: only if it weighs a lot.

u13l6-12.prompt: Marta had written «crypto at most 5%». After a big rise, her crypto now weighs 13.6% without her buying any more. What does she do?
options: She puts more money into crypto because it's doing well
She sells crypto until she's back at 5 %
Nothing: if it's rising, let it keep rising
u13l6-12.explanation: The right one is to rebalance: follow the plan written calmly. Letting it run turns a 5% into the asset that rules the whole portfolio.
feedback: That way she decides with euphoria and raises a risk that was already over her limit.
Good: she follows her plan, keeps part of the gain and goes back to the risk she chose.
Her portfolio is now quite a bit riskier than what she decided calmly.
